en: I have something to tell you openly.
We became relatives through marriage;
Your elder Khan Bakai has his word from then.
He will not greatly humiliate you;
Your own father Temir Khan is still alive.
Your father Temir Khan
Was Bukhara's accomplished ruler.
Simple in thought, pure in thought,
He was an exceptionally worthy man.
He was a khan endowed with grace.
In Temir Khan's household,
Apart from you, Kanykei,
There were twelve daughters.
His rule was renowned among all the people.
Splitting a black hair exactly in two,
Through his impartiality, Temir Khan
Became ruler of great Bukhara.
Having seen twelve pairs of daughters,
He longed for a single son.
When you reach Bukhara and settle,
Do heed what I say:
The only child left by the noble one,
Give him to your royal father, Temir Khan.
If Temir Khan is a man of worth,
Saying, ‘The child left by Manas,’
He will not let him wear dirty clothes,
Or bite the rim of a dirty bowl.
He will not let him feel his orphanhood,
Or let anyone's tongue hurt him.”
So saying, Khan Bakai
Took leave of the orphan.
Speaking thus to the widow,
To royal Bukhara's city,
To her noble Temir Khan,
He gave her a letter plainly written.
“Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
When you travel, do not linger on the road,
Do not camp in an improper place.
Remember, my child, what you have heard;
Do not count those who stray from the path as friends.
If you travel day and night,
Covering ground without sparing your horse,
There is a pass seven days away.
After you cross that pass,
There is no mountain even the size of a saddlecloth,
No ravine even the size of a saddlecloth,
No furrow a plow has entered,
No burrow dug by a marmot.
No wild duck can keep flying there;
The huge black bald-headed vulture
Cannot reach it, its wings exhausted.
Its ravens grow weary flying;
No swift bird crosses above it,
Its wings grow tired and spent.
That desert is eleven days across;
It is a God-stricken land.
You will cross that desert,
Oh, Kanykei, my foal.
If you look beyond it—
There is Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoi.
You will reach Kul-Tokoi.
When you arrive at Kul-Tokoi,
You will rejoice with laughter.
Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoi—
There is snow upon its mountains,
And rooks clamoring in its forest.
There are hares in its hollows,
Wild sheep upon its hills,
Wolves upon its lower slopes,
And deer in its sheltered places.
Its apples ripen and fall to compost.
Choking with grief, crying out,
Mourners have lain there.
Its walnuts ripen and fall to compost,
With streams at their very roots.
Living creatures and flying birds
Have made that place their home.
Its birds hatched in the birches
Are preparing for flight.
Its birds hatched in the poplars,
When I went there, Kanykei,
Were poised, eager to fly.
Lying down to sleep your fill,
Letting your winged steeds graze,
You will stay at Kul-Tokoi.
If you pass Kul-Tokoi safely,
Kanykei, my child, you will attain your desire.
When you go on from there,
Across yellow hills and desert slopes,
Your royal father Temir Khan—
It was Temir Khan's land—
You will reach great Ak-Chii.
When you reached fourteen years,
A lovely girl at play,
When you enjoyed abundant happiness,
Your fine hair as thick as a saddle-girth
You bound snugly upon your crown.
Finding no mountain to dash against,
Finding no foe to battle,
As you roamed the land,
When your imposing head was fair,
When you were Bukhara's ruling maiden,
Against Chubak, son of Khan Akbaltai,
When you were wrestling,
Not yielding for sixty days,
My child, when you were contending,
At the age of fourteen,
When Chubak withdrew, unable to overcome you,
To the leopard Manas
He went at once and told him.
Oh, Kanykei, my foal,
You turned your inclination toward the right.
Beyond there you yourself will know,
Kanykei, my child, the places where you played.”
Unable to linger over farewells,
He shook hands and sped away.
“Farewell, mother, stay safe!” he said.
That elder of yours, Bakai,
Spurred off toward Talas.
Then Kanykei went on in mourning.
To the city of royal Bukhara
Semetey wandered onward.
Your lion-mother Kanykei,
Your precious mother Chyiyrdy,
Past one spur after another,
They went without setting foot there.
To refresh their souls in some resting place,
They did not lie down, but went onward.
Renowned throughout the world,
Your cherished mother Kanykei
Found no room for herself and went on.
Over ridge after rolling ridge
She passed onward.
Truly fleeing till the horses wearied,
She hurried on.
The gold coins and yellow gold they had amassed
She scattered as she went.
That Aman-Jol no human trod,
Your leopard-like widowed warrior
Kept treading onward.
Setting out toward Bukhara,
Proceeding steadfastly without turning aside,
Across pass after pass
Your two mothers went,
Through the brain-boiling desert.
Taitoru and Akborchuk
Swallowed not one gulp of water,
Cropped not one crunch of grass.
Without lying on their sides to sleep their fill,
Wandering toward Bukhara, traveling on,
Nor letting the winged steeds graze,
She carried Semetey before her.
When they reached certain places,
He cried out as they went.
“Do not die, my warrior, my lord!”
Your renowned sister-in-law Kanykei
Grew worn as she went.
The well-fed lamb, that sweet head,
Semetey was beneath her arm.
She fed him meat from their provisions.
The milk poured into the leather flask,
To her only child, whom she counted on,
Semetey, she gave to suck.
The cooked meat upon the bones
She fed to Chyiyrdy.
Finding no rest by day,
Getting no sleep by night,
Never stopping each day,
Taking no time from the daylight,
Traveling day and night,
Covering ground without sparing the horses,
Putting much road behind them,
At Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoi—
At Kul-Tokoi they now arrived and camped.
They called it Father Kul-Tokoi.
Countless saints had spread their hands there;
It was a place where light had poured down.
Blessed place, its apples ripened and fell to compost.
Pure saints and holy elders
Had spent the night there.
Walnuts fell from the trees.
To the woman crying out in anguish,
That Kul-Tokoi where she stood
Appeared like true paradise.
The cuckoo spoke from the plane tree,
The owl called upon its mountain.
There, snowcocks cried from the hills,
From the lower slopes, chukars and birds swooped down.
Nightingales sang from this forest,
Parrots spoke from the willows.
There were living souls and animals;
In Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoi
Everything the Creator made was there.
If you looked just before you,
There were plane trees the size of houses.
Not a cup-sized patch of the plane tree was intact;
Upon every branch there was a nest.
If she looked at one branch,
Kites that flew with drooping wings had nested.
If she looked at another branch,
Blue-mottled-necked jackdaws had nested.
If she looked at another branch,
Rooks with bulging throats had nested.
If she looked toward the lower end,
The fork-tailed one had nested there.
When she looked then,
Every kind of living creature had bred there.
Its birds had hatched in the birches;
When your fierce woman looked,
They stood preparing to fly.
Its birds had hatched in the poplars;
They stood eager to take wing.
Kuleshen's Kul-Tokoi—
When she went into its midst,
Its leaves were like leather.
A saint had lain there;
Its black worms were as big as thumbs.
Kanykei reached the great poplar,
Removed the saddles, leaving the horses bare.
That noble leopard Bakai—
With the great hobbles he had given as a gift,
She hobbled those winged steeds above the hooves.
The white lead rope tied with a loop-knot
She fastened again, drawing them close.
There, in breezy Ken-Ozon,
Those accomplished winged coursers
She entrusted to the great poplar.
The white saddles made by your noble Alake
They each laid beneath their heads.
With their heads toward the qibla,
They lay down to sleep their fill,
Resting their bodies upon their sides,
Sleeping propped upon an elbow,
Taking a quiet nap.
Beseeching her Allah,
The battle-axe left by noble Manas,
Your lion-like sister-in-law Kanykei
Held in her right hand.
After she had dozed a while,
Kanykei woke from sleep with a start.
Alas, that poor handmaid, like a rooster,
Turned onto her right side.
The pain in her chafed feet had eased.
Your mother who traveled the road
Opened her eyes, small as dough pellets.
When she rose from sleep, awake,
Those winged steeds, their flesh restored,
Were tossing wildly,
Chewing their bits and straining.
Laying back their right ears,
The coursers snorted,
The crust of the black earth
They flung up toward the sky.
When your sister-in-law rose from sleep,
Stars trembled in the heavens,
One by one toward the qibla.
